text:
A: Hiya, can you hear me alright?
B: Yes, hi! I can hear you fine. I'm Claire.
A: I'm Megan. Sorry, I'm a bit nervous, I always think I'm doing these wrong.
B: Oh, I think we all are. That puzzle at the start threw me completely.
A: Oh my God, same. I read the instructions twice and still wasn't sure. Erm, where are you based?
B: Catford, South East London. You?
A: Stockton-on-Tees. Norton, technically, if that makes sense. North East, but not Newcastle.
B: Not Newcastle, noted. I won't say Geordie.
A: Thank you! People always do. So what do you do?
B: I'm a housing officer for a housing association. I look after about three hundred flats, so it's home visits, rent arrears, repairs, people falling out with their neighbours. Quite a lot of listening, really. What about you? I guessed nursing from your photo, I don't know why.
A: Close! I'm doing diagnostic radiography at Teesside, second year. So X-rays, basically, and then CT and things later. I've got placements at James Cook and North Tees, so it's sort of half uni, half hospital.
B: Oh, that's interesting. Do you like the hospital side?
A: I do, yeah. I get dead anxious before placements, like I can't sleep the night before sometimes, but once I'm there it's fine. I'm good with the older patients, they're usually nervous as well, so we're nervous together. My shifts start at half seven, so I'm up at six, and the parking at James Cook is shocking, honestly.
B: Hospital parking, that's universal, isn't it? Was it always radiography for you?
A: Erm, no, not really. I started Biomedical Science at eighteen and left after the first year, it felt a bit too abstract. Then I worked in a pharmacy for nearly three years. So I'm kind of a bit behind, if that makes sense.
B: Behind? I don't think that's behind at all. I did my housing qualification part-time in my thirties, and half the people on it were career changers. Working in a pharmacy probably makes you better at the patient bit, you know?
A: Yeah, that's what my mam says. And the paperwork. I'm quite fussy about request forms because of the pharmacy.
B: That's a good thing to be fussy about. I'm the same with case notes. Colleagues tease me, but then they come and ask me what they wrote.
A: Ha, yeah. Is your job quite stressful, then?
B: Erm, sometimes, yeah. Damp and mould cases, families squashed into one-beds. You do take some of it home. I swim in the mornings, which helps clear my head.
A: I do parkrun, when I'm not on placement. Preston Park, Saturday mornings. I'm on week five of my running plan as well.
B: Week five, that's good going. I gave up running, dodgy knee. Do you live near the hospital?
A: No, I'm at home with my mam and stepdad and my little brother. He's sixteen and eats everything in the fridge. My mam's done mince and dumplings for tea tonight, so I'll have to be quick.
B: Mince and dumplings, that sounds lovely. My husband works evenings so I mostly cook dinner for one.
A: Oh, that's a shame. Is that a lot of cooking for one person?
B: Too much, usually. I make Ottolenghi things that take three hours and then eat them for four days.
A: Sorry, I'm just thinking, I don't even know what Ottolenghi is. Is that a person?
B: It is, yes, a chef. Lots of pomegranate. You're not missing much on a Tuesday.
A: I'll stick with my chicken and rice in a tub, I think.
B: Honestly, that sounds very sensible. I think we're nearly out of time.
A: Oh, already? It's been really nice, thank you.
B: You too, Megan. Good luck with placement.
